boardQuestions.question: Differentiate between dominant and recessive traits with one example of each.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) A dominant trait is expressed even when only one copy of its allele is present in the pair; it masks the other allele. 2) A recessive trait is expressed only when both alleles of the pair are of the recessive form. 3) Example: in pea plants, tallness is dominant over dwarfness, so a plant with Tt genotype is tall, while dwarfness appears only in tt plants. 4) In Mendel's cross, the F1 plants (Tt) were all tall, proving that tallness is dominant and dwarfness is recessive.

boardQuestions.question: Differentiate between acquired and inherited traits with one example each. Why are acquired traits not inherited?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Acquired traits develop during the lifetime of an organism due to environment or use, for example the low weight of a starved beetle. 2) Inherited traits are present in the DNA of germ cells and pass from parents to offspring, for example eye colour or blood group. 3) Acquired traits are not inherited because they change only the body (somatic) cells and never change germ cell DNA. 4) Since only germ cell DNA reaches the next generation, changes like cut tails of mice are never inherited.

boardQuestions.question: How are traits expressed through genes? Explain with the example of tallness and dwarfness in pea plants.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) A gene is a segment of DNA that provides the information for making a particular protein or enzyme. 2) For the height trait, one version of the gene makes an efficient enzyme that helps the plant produce a plant hormone needed for growth; the other version makes a less efficient form of this enzyme. 3) In a tall pea plant the efficient enzyme makes enough hormone, so the plant grows tall; in the dwarf plant the less efficient enzyme makes less hormone, so growth remains limited and the plant stays dwarf. 4) Thus a trait depends on the protein or enzyme a gene produces, and a single gene pair can decide the visible character of the plant. 5) Every cell carries two copies of each gene because chromosomes come in pairs, one set from each parent.

boardQuestions.question: How is the sex of a child determined in human beings? Describe the cross and state the probability of a boy or a girl.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes; 22 pairs are autosomes and one pair is the sex chromosome pair. 2) Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). 3) Every egg produced by the mother carries one X chromosome. 4) Sperms produced by the father carry either X or Y chromosome in roughly equal numbers. 5) If an X sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XX and the child is a girl; if a Y sperm fertilises it, the zygote is XY and the child is a boy. 6) Since half the sperms carry X and half carry Y, the probability of a boy or a girl is about 50 percent each; hence the father, not the mother, determines the sex of the child.

boardQuestions.question: Describe Mendel's monohybrid cross from the parental generation to F2 with the help of a Punnett square (describe it in words), state the F1 and F2 ratios, and explain the laws of dominance and segregation shown by this experiment.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Monohybrid cross: Mendel crossed pure tall pea plants (TT) with pure dwarf plants (tt); both parents bred true for generations. 2) Gametes: the tall parent produced gametes with T only, and the dwarf parent produced gametes with t only. 3) F1 generation: all offspring were Tt and appeared tall; the dwarf character disappeared, showing that tallness is dominant and dwarfness is recessive; this is the law of dominance. 4) Mendel then self-pollinated the F1 tall plants. 5) Gametes of F1: each F1 plant formed two kinds of gametes, T and t, in equal numbers, because the two alleles separate during gamete formation; this is the law of segregation. 6) Punnett square described: make a 2 by 2 grid; write T and t of one parent on top and T and t of the other on the side; the four boxes give TT, Tt, tT and tt. 7) F2 results: three of the four plants are tall (TT, Tt, tT) and one is dwarf (tt), so the phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf. 8) Genotypic ratio: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, showing that genotypes differ even when phenotypes look alike. 9) Interpretation: the dwarf trait did not vanish in F1; it was merely hidden and reappeared in F2, proving that traits are controlled by separate units (genes) which do not blend. 10) Significance: segregation explains why each parent passes only one allele of a pair to each offspring, and dominance explains which allele is seen in the heterozygote.

boardQuestions.question: Describe Mendel's dihybrid cross in pea plants up to the F2 generation, derive the phenotypic ratio, and explain the law of independent assortment.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Dihybrid cross: Mendel crossed pea plants having pure round and yellow seeds (RRYY) with plants having wrinkled and green seeds (rryy). 2) Gametes: the first parent produced only RY gametes and the second only ry gametes. 3) F1 generation: all offspring were RrYy and had round and yellow seeds, showing that round dominates wrinkled and yellow dominates green. 4) Self-pollination of F1: each F1 plant formed four kinds of gametes in equal numbers - RY, Ry, rY and ry - because the alleles of the two genes assorted independently during gamete formation. 5) Punnett square described: a 4 by 4 grid with RY, Ry, rY and ry written on both sides gives 16 boxes. 6) F2 phenotypes: 9 round-yellow, 3 round-green, 3 wrinkled-yellow and 1 wrinkled-green; phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1. 7) New combinations: round-green (Rryy) and wrinkled-yellow (rrYy) were not present in the parents, yet they appeared in F2. 8) Law of independent assortment: the two pairs of contrasting traits are inherited independently of each other because the alleles of different genes separate into gametes without influencing each other. 9) Interpretation: the appearance of new combinations proves that the genes for seed shape and seed colour are separate units that can combine freely. 10) Check: 9 plus 3 plus 3 plus 1 equals 16, matching the 16 boxes of the Punnett square; this ratio is the classic proof of independent assortment in dihybrid inheritance.

boardQuestions.question: Read the passage: A plant breeder crossed pure-breeding pea plants having round and yellow seeds with pure-breeding plants having wrinkled and green seeds. All the F1 plants produced round and yellow seeds. When he self-pollinated the F1 plants, the F2 generation showed four kinds of seeds: round-yellow, round-green, wrinkled-yellow and wrinkled-green in the ratio 9:3:3:1. (a) Why did all the F1 plants show round and yellow seeds? (b) Which seed types in F2 were absent in the parents, and what does their appearance prove? (c) Write the genotypes possible for each of the four F2 seed types and state Mendel's law demonstrated by this experiment.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Roundness is dominant over wrinkledness and yellow is dominant over green; the F1 plants received one dominant allele of each pair (RrYy), so only the dominant characters, round and yellow, were visible. 2) The recessive alleles r and y remained hidden in the F1 genotype but were carried safely into the gametes. 3) (b) Round-green and wrinkled-yellow seeds were absent in the original parents, yet they appeared in the F2 generation. 4) Their appearance proves that the gene for seed shape and the gene for seed colour are inherited independently, so new combinations can form when the F1 gametes fuse in all possible ways. 5) (c) Genotypes: round-yellow can be RRYY, RrYY, RRYy or RrYy (9 plants in all); round-green is Rryy (3 plants); wrinkled-yellow is rrYy (3 plants); wrinkled-green is rryy (1 plant). 6) The classic ratio 9:3:3:1 comes from the 16 boxes of the F1 self-cross Punnett square, with gametes RY, Ry, rY and ry on both sides. 7) Law demonstrated: Mendel's law of independent assortment, because the alleles of seed shape and seed colour separated into gametes without influencing each other, along with the law of dominance seen in the F1. 8) Practical value: breeders use such crosses to combine useful traits like high yield and disease resistance into one variety, relying on the independent assortment of genes.

chapters.title: Our Environment
chapters.summary: An ecosystem consists of all interacting living organisms in an area along with their non-living surroundings, connected by food chains and food webs. Energy flows in one direction through trophic levels with about ten percent transferred at each step, while nutrients are recycled by decomposers. The chapter also covers ozone layer depletion by CFCs and the management of biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes.
hotTopics: Food chain, food web and trophic levels
Ten percent law with numerical problems
Ecosystem components and role of decomposers

sections.heading: Ecosystem and Its Components
points: An ecosystem is made of all the interacting organisms in an area together with their physical surroundings, which include abiotic components like air, water, soil, temperature and light.
Producers: green plants and algae (autotrophs) that trap sunlight and make food by photosynthesis; they form the energy base of every ecosystem.
Consumers: organisms that depend on others for food - herbivores (plant eaters) are primary consumers, small carnivores are secondary consumers, and big carnivores are top or tertiary consumers.
Decomposers: bacteria and fungi that break down complex dead remains into simple inorganic substances, returning nutrients to the soil for reuse by plants.
Decomposers are the cleaning crew of nature; without them dead matter would pile up, nutrients would never return to the soil and the nutrient cycle would stop.
Ecosystems may be natural like forests, ponds and lakes, or artificial like aquariums, gardens and crop fields.

keyTerms.meaning: All the interacting organisms in an area together with their non-living physical surroundings.
Autotrophic organisms like green plants that make food from sunlight and form the first trophic level.
Saprotrophic organisms like bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.

sections.trick: P-C-D ladder: Producers produce, Consumers consume, Decomposers decompose and recycle; no D in the team means no soil fertility ever.
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks: what happens if decomposers are removed from an ecosystem (2-3 marks), or to classify a given list of organisms as producers, consumers and decomposers.

sections.heading: Food Chains and Food Webs
points: A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms showing who eats whom, for example grass -> deer -> lion or grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk.
Arrows in a food chain point from the organism being eaten to the one that eats it, showing the direction of energy flow.
Each step of a food chain is a trophic level: producers form the first level, herbivores the second, small carnivores the third and larger carnivores the fourth.
A food web is the network of many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, formed because most organisms eat more than one kind of food.
Food webs make ecosystems stable: if one food source becomes scarce, a consumer can switch to another, so no population depends on a single chain.
Because energy is lost at every trophic level, food chains rarely exceed four or five steps, and the number of individuals decreases at higher levels.

keyTerms.meaning: A step-by-step sequence of organisms in which each organism is eaten by the next, showing energy flow.
The interconnected network of many food chains in an ecosystem.
The position of an organism in a food chain, decided by its source of food and energy.

sections.trick: Arrows aim at the eater: grass -> deer -> lion; memorise the NCERT five-step chain G-H-F-S-H (grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk) with levels 1 to 5.
sections.examPointer: Expect: construct a four-level food chain and name each trophic level, or explain why a food web is more realistic and stable than a single food chain.

sections.heading: Energy Flow and the Ten Percent Law
points: Energy enters the ecosystem as sunlight fixed by producers during photosynthesis and then flows only in one direction, from producers to consumers; it is never cycled back.
Ten percent law: only about ten percent of the energy stored in one trophic level is passed on to the next trophic level.
Numerical example: producers 10,000 J -> herbivores 1,000 J -> small carnivores 100 J -> top carnivores 10 J; each step loses ninety percent of the energy as heat and in life processes.
Due to this steep energy loss, food chains are short and the population of top carnivores is always small.

Harmful non-biodegradable chemicals like pesticides, which cannot be degraded or excreted completely, keep accumulating in body tissues and become most concentrated in top consumers; this is biological magnification.
Energy flow is one-way while nutrients are cycled back by decomposers; this difference explains why ecosystems need constant sunlight but recycle matter.

keyTerms.meaning: The rule that only about 10 percent of the energy of one trophic level is transferred to the next level.
The progressive increase in the concentration of harmful non-biodegradable chemicals at successively higher trophic levels.
The one-way movement of energy from producers to consumers, which can never be reversed or recycled.

sections.trick: Chop one zero at every step: 10,000 -> 1,000 -> 100 -> 10 J, the ten percent staircase; energy is a one-way street, matter is a round trip.
sections.examPointer: The classic numerical: calculate the energy at the third or fourth trophic level when energy at producers is given; also define biomagnification and explain why food chains are short.

sections.heading: Ozone Layer Depletion
points: Ozone (O3) is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms; most of the ozone lies high up in the atmosphere as a layer called the ozone layer.
The ozone layer absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations from the sun and stops them from reaching the Earth's surface.
UV radiation can cause skin cancer and cataract, weaken the immune system, and also damage crops and aquatic life.
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays, release reactive chlorine atoms in the upper atmosphere that break ozone molecules and deplete the layer.
Ozone depletion is a global problem, and worldwide measures such as banning and phasing out CFCs are being taken to protect the layer.

keyTerms.meaning: A molecule of three oxygen atoms (O3) that forms a protective layer in the upper atmosphere.
Chlorofluorocarbons, synthetic gases used in refrigerators and sprays, whose chlorine destroys ozone molecules.
Harmful rays from the sun that the ozone layer absorbs, protecting living beings from skin cancer and cataract.

sections.trick: O3 is the O-shield of the sky; CFC means Chlorine From Coolers (fridges and ACs) that punches holes in the sun umbrella.
sections.examPointer: Common 2-3 marker: where is ozone found, what is its function, which chemicals deplete it, and what harms follow when UV reaches the Earth.

sections.heading: Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Wastes
points: Biodegradable wastes can be broken down into simple, harmless substances by decomposers; examples: vegetable peels, paper, cotton cloth, wood and cow dung.
Non-biodegradable wastes cannot be decomposed by microbes and persist for very long periods; examples: plastics, polybags, glass, aluminium cans and certain pesticides.
Biodegradable waste can be converted into compost or biogas, returning nutrients to the soil and producing useful energy.
Non-biodegradable waste accumulates in the environment, chokes drains, pollutes soil and water, harms animals that swallow plastic and enters food chains through biological magnification.
Segregating garbage at the source into wet (biodegradable) and dry (non-biodegradable) bins makes composting and recycling much easier.

keyTerms.meaning: Waste that decomposers can break down into simple natural substances, like food scraps and paper.
Waste that cannot be broken down by microbes and remains in the environment, like plastic and glass.
Nutrient-rich manure formed by the controlled decomposition of biodegradable waste.

sections.trick: Bio = bite-able by bacteria (peels, paper, dung); Non-bio = never bite-able (plastic, glass) - bin them separately: wet bin, dry bin.
sections.examPointer: Asked: give two examples of each type with reasons, explain why plastics are dangerous, or design a two-bin segregation plan for a household (2-3 marks).

sections.heading: Managing Garbage - The 3R Way and Our Role
points: 3R principle: Reduce (create less waste and avoid unnecessary packaging), Reuse (use things again like bottles and jars), Recycle (send paper, glass and metals to factories to be made into new products).
Composting and vermicomposting: biodegradable waste decomposed in pits or with the help of earthworms into rich manure for gardens and fields.
Recyclable dry waste should go to recycling units, and only the small leftover fraction should reach sanitary landfills.
Open burning of plastic and rubber releases toxic fumes and must be avoided; single-use plastics should be refused.
Unmanaged garbage breeds flies, mosquitoes and rodents, spreads diseases and blocks drains, causing water pollution and flooding.
Every individual can help: separate wet and dry waste at home, compost kitchen waste, carry cloth bags, save paper by using both sides, and encourage neighbours to follow the same habits.

keyTerms.meaning: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle - the three steps to minimise waste, applied in that order of preference.
Conversion of biodegradable waste into manure using earthworms.
A specially designed site where residual non-recyclable waste is buried safely without polluting the surroundings.

sections.trick: R-order matters: Reduce before Reuse before Recycle - not creating waste saves the most; wet waste to compost, dry waste to the recycle bin.
sections.examPointer: Expect: explain the 3R principle with one example of each, suggest a garbage disposal plan for a locality, or list individual actions for waste management (often a CASE question).

mcqs.explanation: Working backwards by the ten percent law: 10 J at hawk, 100 J at snake, 1,000 J at frog, 10,000 J at grasshopper and 100,000 J at grass.

options: Top carnivores of the food chain
mcqs.explanation: Non-degradable pesticides accumulate progressively at each trophic level and are most concentrated in top consumers; this is biological magnification.

boardQuestions.question: What are trophic levels? Give an example of a food chain and name the trophic levels in it.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) A trophic level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain, based on its source of food and energy. 2) Example food chain: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk. 3) Grass is the producer at the first trophic level. 4) The grasshopper is the herbivore at the second trophic level, the frog is the small carnivore at the third, the snake at the fourth and the hawk is the top carnivore at the fifth level.

boardQuestions.question: Differentiate between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances with two examples of each.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Biodegradable substances can be broken down into simple harmless substances by decomposers like bacteria and fungi; examples: vegetable peels and paper. 2) Non-biodegradable substances cannot be broken down by decomposers and remain in the environment for a very long time; examples: plastics and glass bottles. 3) Biodegradable waste can be converted into compost or biogas, while non-biodegradable waste accumulates and pollutes soil and water, so it must be recycled or disposed of safely. 4) This difference decides how each type of garbage should be handled.

boardQuestions.question: State the ten percent law of energy flow. If 10,000 J of energy is available to producers, calculate the energy available to the second and third trophic levels, and explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five steps.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Ten percent law: only about ten percent of the energy stored in the organisms of one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level; the rest is lost in life processes and as heat. 2) Calculation: producers 10,000 J -> herbivores (second trophic level) 1,000 J -> small carnivores (third trophic level) 100 J -> top carnivores (fourth level) only 10 J. 3) Because almost ninety percent of the energy is lost at each step, the energy remaining after a few levels becomes too small to support more organisms. 4) Hence food chains are usually short, rarely exceeding four or five steps, and top carnivores are always few in number.

boardQuestions.question: Where is the ozone layer found and why is it important? Name the chemicals that deplete it and suggest one step to protect it.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Ozone is a molecule of three oxygen atoms (O3); most of the ozone is found high up in the atmosphere as a layer called the ozone layer. 2) Importance: it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations coming from the sun and stops them from reaching the Earth's surface. 3) UV rays can cause skin cancer and cataract, damage the immune system and harm crops and aquatic life, so the ozone layer acts as a protective shield for all life. 4) Depleting chemicals: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays release reactive chlorine in the upper atmosphere, which breaks ozone molecules and thins the layer. 5) Protective step: phase out and avoid CFC-based products, use CFC-free refrigerants, and support international bans on ozone-harming chemicals.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the components of an ecosystem with the special role of decomposers. Construct a food web (describe it in words) for a garden ecosystem and explain why a food web is more realistic than a single food chain.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Ecosystem: all the interacting organisms in an area together with the non-living surroundings like air, water, soil, temperature and light. 2) Biotic components: producers, consumers and decomposers. 3) Producers: green plants and algae that trap sunlight and make food by photosynthesis; they form the energy base of the ecosystem. 4) Consumers: herbivores eat plants (primary consumers), small carnivores eat herbivores (secondary consumers), and top carnivores occupy the highest level. 5) Decomposers: bacteria and fungi that break down dead bodies and wastes into simple inorganic substances, returning nutrients to the soil for reuse by plants. 6) Role of decomposers: without them dead matter would pile up and nutrients would never return to the soil, so the nutrient cycle would stop and the ecosystem would collapse. 7) Garden food web described: grass and shrubs are eaten by grasshoppers and rabbits; grasshoppers are eaten by frogs and birds; rabbits are eaten by snakes and hawks; snakes are also eaten by hawks; dead leaves are broken down by fungi and earthworms. 8) Since each organism eats more than one kind of food, all these chains interconnect into a web: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk and grass -> rabbit -> hawk are two chains sharing the same hawk. 9) Advantage of a web: if one food source becomes scarce, consumers switch to another, so populations do not collapse; the web gives stability to the ecosystem, while a single food chain is fragile.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the 3R principle of waste management with examples. Describe how garbage should be disposed of in a locality and list the actions individuals can take to manage waste.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) 3R stands for Reduce, Reuse and Recycle, applied in that order of preference. 2) Reduce: cut down the amount of waste created, for example buying products with less packaging, refusing polybags and using cloth bags, and avoiding single-use plastic items. 3) Reuse: use a thing again instead of throwing it away, for example refilling glass or plastic bottles, reusing jars for storage and donating old clothes and books. 4) Recycle: send used materials like paper, glass, metal and some plastics to factories where they are processed into new products, saving raw materials and energy. 5) Segregation: households should keep two bins, one for wet biodegradable waste like peels and leftover food, and one for dry non-biodegradable waste like plastics, paper and metal. 6) Disposal methods: biodegradable waste can be composted in pits or vermicomposted using earthworms to make manure; dry recyclable waste goes to recycling units; the small remaining fraction goes to sanitary landfills. 7) Avoid open burning: burning plastic and rubber releases poisonous gases and should never be done; batteries and e-waste need special collection points. 8) Individual actions: separate wet and dry waste at home, compost kitchen waste, carry cloth bags, save paper by using both sides, avoid packaged and single-use items, and encourage family and neighbours to follow the same habits. 9) Benefit: proper waste management keeps soil, water and air clean, prevents diseases spread by flies and rodents, and conserves resources for future generations.

boardQuestions.question: Read the passage: In a village, farmers grew crops around a pond. The pond contained algae and small aquatic plants, which were eaten by small fish; big fish ate the small fish, and pond herons ate the big fish. For many years the farmers sprayed a non-biodegradable pesticide on the fields, and some of it washed into the pond. Tests done after several years showed the pesticide concentration to be highest in the herons. (a) Construct the aquatic food chain described and name the trophic levels. (b) Explain why the pesticide concentration was highest in the herons even though they never touched the sprayed fields. (c) If the energy stored in the aquatic plants is 50,000 J, calculate the energy reaching the herons, and state one step the village can take to reduce this pesticide problem.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Food chain: aquatic plants and algae (producers, first trophic level) -> small fish (herbivores, second level) -> big fish (carnivores, third level) -> pond herons (top carnivores, fourth level). 2) (b) The pesticide is non-biodegradable, so it is not broken down or excreted completely by the organisms that take it in. 3) It enters the pond water, is absorbed by plants, then passes to small fish, then big fish and finally herons; at every step it accumulates in the body tissues. 4) Since it moves up the food chain and becomes more and more concentrated, the top consumers, the herons, carry the highest amount; this progressive increase of harmful chemicals is called biological magnification. 5) (c) Calculation by the ten percent law: plants 50,000 J -> small fish 5,000 J -> big fish 500 J -> herons 50 J. 6) Only about ten percent of the energy passes to the next level, so herons receive roughly 50 J of energy from the 50,000 J fixed by the plants. 7) This steep loss of energy also explains why herons, as top consumers, are few in number. 8) Step for the village: stop or minimise the spraying of non-biodegradable pesticides and switch to biodegradable or biological pest control methods, keeping the pond water free of chemical runoff. 9) Learning point: energy flows one way and decreases along a chain, while non-biodegradable harmful substances flow the same way but increase in concentration, endangering top carnivores like herons, fish-eating birds and even humans.
